suggestions.rationale: Sphincter-cutting treatment for anal fistula, particularly fistulotomy and related procedures that divide continence muscle, can cause postoperative continence impairment. A systematic review of simple fistula-in-ano reported postoperative continence impairment after sphincter-cutting procedures and emphasized that the underlying study quality was generally low. This supports a treatment-complication pathway only when the individual underwent a documented sphincter-involving fistula procedure and fecal incontinence began or materially worsened afterward; anal fistula by itself, and sphincter-sparing treatment without a compatible complication, should not be treated as sufficient evidence of causation.

pathwayIntelligence.causalChain: Anal fistula → documented sphincter-cutting or sphincter-involving treatment, if performed → postoperative sphincter/continence impairment → clinically confirmed fecal incontinence.
developmentQuestions: What fistula anatomy was documented, including tract height, sphincter involvement, complexity, recurrence, and prior procedures?
Which procedure was performed, and did operative records document division or injury of internal or external anal sphincter muscle?
What was baseline continence before treatment, and did fecal incontinence begin or materially worsen after the procedure?
What do anorectal examination, manometry, endoanal ultrasound, or other applicable tests show about postoperative sphincter integrity and function?

Which competing causes of incontinence, including preexisting sphincter injury, inflammatory bowel disease, neuropathy, diarrhea, pelvic-floor dysfunction, or other anorectal surgery, should be addressed?
issuesToResolve: The evidence is treatment-specific and should not be generalized from sphincter-cutting procedures to every anal fistula or every sphincter-sparing intervention.

The systematic-review evidence is generally low quality, so operative anatomy, baseline continence, postoperative chronology, objective sphincter findings, and alternative causes are especially important.

evidenceGaps: Operative reports identifying fistula anatomy and the exact treatment performed
Anorectal examination and sphincter imaging/function testing when clinically indicated
Documentation of postoperative onset or worsening and subsequent treatment course
Colorectal opinion addressing procedure-related sphincter injury and competing causes of fecal incontinence

sourceReferences.citation: Litta F et al. Tech Coloproctol. 2021;25(4):385-399. PMID 33387100
sourceReferences.note: Systematic review of 66 studies reported postoperative continence impairment in 12.7% of patients undergoing sphincter-cutting treatment for simple anal fistula; study quality was generally low. Supports a procedure-specific continence-complication pathway, not automatic attribution from the fistula diagnosis itself.
sourceReferences.sourceLocator: PMID 33387100; abstract: 66 eligible studies; 4,883 sphincter-cutting procedures, mainly fistulotomy; postoperative continence impairment 12.7%; study quality generally low
